title: Wrangler accepts 19 hidden flags whether they do anything
description: Nineteen hidden flags in one CLI, and the control that tells an option being accepted apart from an option doing anything.
bodyHtml:
Wrangler accepts 19 hidden flags whether they do anything

Wrangler 4.125.0 carries nineteen flags marked hidden, so they appear in no help output and no documentation page. Reading them is easy. The hard part is that an option a tool silently ignores and an option it honours produce the same exit code, the same output, and the same success. This page is about the control that separates those two, why it usually costs nothing, and four times the difference decided something real on this site.

The inventory

Every flag below was pulled out of the shipped bundle by matching option definitions that carry hidden: true, then read back with its own description. Filter by what it is for.

19 hidden flags5 of 19 hidden flags4 of 19 hidden flags2 of 19 hidden flags6 of 19 hidden flags3 of 19 hidden flags3 of 19 hidden flags1 of 19 hidden flags
flagaliasgroupwhat it says it does
--experimental-new-config--x-new-configconfig[experimental] Use cloudflare.config.ts and wrangler.config.ts
--experimental-cf-build-output--x-cf-build-outputconfig[experimental] Emit a Build Output Specification directory under .cloudflare/output/ (requires --experimental-new-config)
--experimental-auto-create--x-auto-createreleaseAutomatically provision draft bindings with new resources
--experimental-provisionreleaseNo description in the definition. Pinned off here alongside auto-create, because no deploy path on this account may create resources.
--max-versionsreleaseMaximum allowed versions to select. Defaults to 2, and its own comment says the limit is server side.
--experimental-deploy-helpers--x-deploy-helpersreleaseExperimental: Gates refactored deploy/upload path
--experimental-include-runtime--x-include-runtimetypesThe path of the generated runtime types file
--enable-containerscontainersWhether to build and enable containers during development
--config-file-FcontainersSets ssh -F: specify an alternative per-user ssh configuration file
--identity-file-icontainersSets ssh -i: select a file from which the identity for public key authentication is read
--escape-charcontainersSets ssh -e: set the escape character for sessions with a pty
--log-filecontainersSets ssh -E: append debug logs to log_file instead of standard error
--mac-speccontainersSets ssh -m: a comma separated list of message authentication code algorithms, in order of preference
--delegate-c3--c3setupDelegate to Create Cloudflare CLI (C3)
--install-wranglersetupInstall Wrangler during project setup
--completion-messagesetupDisplay a message with deployment details after wrangler setup is complete
--node-compatlegacyEnable Node.js compatibility
--site-includelegacyWorkers Sites: gitignore style patterns; only matched items will be uploaded
--site-excludelegacyWorkers Sites: gitignore style patterns; matched items are skipped

Marked rows are the ones that touch this site. The rest are here so the list is the whole list: a survey that reports only the interesting rows cannot tell you how many rows it skipped.

Two questions, and only one of them is free

When you find an undocumented option, there are two separate things to establish, and reading the docs answers neither.

Is it accepted? Does the tool recognise the key at all, or is it dropping an unknown name on the floor? Does it work? Does accepting the key change the behaviour the flag claims to change.

The first question is usually free, and people skip it. A tool with strict argument parsing answers it through its exit code alone, with no work performed and nothing deployed:

$ wrangler deploy --x-bogus-flag ; echo $?
1
$ wrangler deploy --x-provision=false --dry-run ; echo $?
0

Two commands, no account touched, and the answer is decisive: wrangler validates flag names, so a flag it accepts is a flag it knows. Run that before trusting any option a help page omits.

The second question costs a real run, and its answer is worth much less than it looks like when the failure mode is silence.

When silence is the failure mode

Four cases from this site, each of which cost time in proportion to how late the control was run.

A payload schema that refuses unknown keys

Cloudflare's Browser Run binding takes a JSON payload. A launch post described selecting a rendering engine with one extra key; the Quick Actions reference did not list it. Sending it answered:

{"code":"unrecognized_keys","keys":["browser"]}

An invented engine name returned the byte-identical error. The schema is closed, so it refuses the option rather than failing on the value, and a closed schema is a gift: it answers "is this accepted" for free, every time, with no render performed and no browser minutes spent.

The same feature then produced the opposite trap through the REST door, where the parameter is merely ignored. A 200 came back either way, so the code labelled the render with the engine it had asked for. On a page whose premise is showing what a machine actually saw, that label was a claim the code never checked. It reads kitesurf-requested now.

A compression option three runtimes disagree about

Dictionary compression takes a dictionary option. Node 26 honours it. Workers ignore it for zstd and say nothing. Bun ignored it through 1.3.14 and fixed it in oven-sh/bun#34427. Every one of those failures is silent, because a frame compressed without a dictionary still decodes perfectly with one. Nothing throws. The only symptom is a byte count that never got smaller.

The control is four lines and it needs no deploy: compress one target three times, with no dictionary, with the right one, and with a deliberately wrong one. An engine that honours the option prints a smaller number for the right dictionary alone. An engine that ignores it prints the same number three times.

engineno dictionaryright dictionaryverdict
node 2670 B18 Bhonours it
workerdsame number three timesignores it
bun through 1.3.14same number three timesignored it

Sending the option and reading the exit code would have passed on all three.

A key that is accepted and still unmeasured

The Browser Run payload takes a waitForTimeout. Whether the binding accepts the key was answered for free, using the closed schema above: send it alongside a deliberately invalid URL, and a bogus key comes back as unrecognized_keys while an accepted one leaves only the URL error. Three keys passed that test individually and together.

Whether the capture actually waits out the timeout is a different question, it needs a real render, and it is still open. Both halves are written down separately for that reason. An entry claiming the key works, on evidence that only shows it is accepted, is the exact error this page is about.

A path that routes either way

The engine selector above only functions on one of two URL spellings. Both route. Probed unauthenticated against a real account, each answers 10000 Authentication error rather than 7003 Could not route to. So the wrong path costs the feature, silently: no error, no retry, no log line. One reference page documents the selector on the newer spelling while older pages show the other, so reading either one alone hands you a path that looks right.

A flag that proves the limit is somewhere else

Among the nineteen is --max-versions, on the command that shifts production traffic between Worker versions. This site's release script walks a version to 10%, then 50%, then 100%, and it can only ever name two versions in a step, which shapes the whole procedure: a ramp starting from a three-way split has to drop one of them. The obvious hope is that a hidden flag raises the ceiling. The definition answers it without a single request:

"max-versions": {
  hidden: true,
  // experimental, not supported long-term
  describe: "Maximum allowed versions to select",
  type: "number",
  default: 2
  // (when server-side limitation is lifted, we can update this
  //  default or just remove the option entirely)
}

The comment is the finding. The cap lives on the server and this flag is the client's mirror of it, so raising the number locally buys an error instead of a wider split. That is a real answer, arrived at by reading rather than by deploying, and it retires a question that had been open on the strength of a guess.

A flag that looks like the fix and is not one

This site has a documented failure where a gradual deployment splits asset requests: a document served by one version asks for a content-hashed asset only the other version built, and gets a 404. So --old-asset-ttl, described as "expire old assets in given seconds rather than immediate deletion", reads like the exact repair.

It is threaded into one place in the entire codebase, and that place is the sync routine for the legacy Workers Sites layer, the retired KV-namespace mechanism that predates the modern assets binding this site uses. The flag would apply to a system that is not running here.

Fifteen minutes of reading, and the answer arrives before any config changes. Had it been adopted on the strength of its description, it would have shipped, changed nothing, and become the fix everyone believed was already in place.

Pick a situation, get the control

The shape of the doubt decides the experiment. Choose what you are looking at:

Run it three ways and compare the number

An engine that ignores an option produces output identical to one that never received it, and the output still works. So do not ask whether it succeeded. Ask whether the thing the option claims to change actually changed, against a case where it could not have.

compress(target)                 # no option
compress(target, opt: correct)   # the option, correct value
compress(target, opt: wrong)     # the option, useless value
what you seewhat it means
all three identicalthe option is being dropped
correct one smaller, wrong one matches the firstthe option is honoured
correct and wrong both differ from the firstsomething reads the option and your model of it is off

Cost: three local runs, no deploy. This is the control that separates node, workerd and bun on the same option.

Send a key you invented, next to a request that fails anyway

A closed schema validates the shape before it does any work, which makes it the cheapest oracle you will ever get. Pair the probe with a deliberately invalid input so nothing can execute even if the key is accepted.

send({ url: "not-a-url", definitely_not_a_key_xyz: 1 })
send({ url: "not-a-url", theKeyYouAreUnsure: 1 })
what you seewhat it means
first names your bogus key, second reports only the url errorthe key is accepted, and the schema is closed
both report only the url errorthe schema is open, so acceptance proves nothing
both name the bogus keyyour unsure key is being rejected too

Cost: two rejected requests. Nothing renders, nothing is billed, and it answers acceptance completely.

Read the exit code on a name that cannot exist

Argument parsers either validate names or ignore them. One invented flag tells you which, and it tells you before you have trusted a real one.

tool command --x-bogus-flag ; echo $?
tool command --the-real-flag=false --dry-run ; echo $?
what you seewhat it means
1 then 0names are validated, so an accepted flag is a known flag
0 then 0unknown names are ignored, and acceptance means nothing at all
1 then 1the real flag is being rejected too, so check the spelling and the subcommand

Cost: one exit code. Pair it with --dry-run so the second command performs no work.

Compare the errors, rather than the successes

When an old and a new URL spelling both respond, a success on either one proves nothing about which is live. The distinguishing signal lives in what each one says when it refuses, and an unauthenticated request is enough to get it.

curl -s https://api/OLD-SPELLING/action   # unauthenticated
curl -s https://api/NEW-SPELLING/action   # unauthenticated
what you seewhat it means
both report an auth errorboth spellings route, so pick the one the feature's own page documents
one reports could-not-routethat spelling is dead and the choice is made for you
one reports auth and the other 404ssame conclusion, through a different status

Cost: two unauthenticated requests. No credential, so this one is safe to run against somebody else's API.

The rule this leaves

On a closed schema, "is this accepted" and "does this work" are two questions, and the first one is free. Ask it first, always, because it costs an exit code and it eliminates the most common way an undocumented option wastes a week: being quietly dropped while everything around it reports success.

Then be careful about what a success proves. A 200 from an endpoint that ignores unknown parameters is indistinguishable from a 200 from an endpoint that honoured yours. When you cannot tell those apart, the honest move is to label the result with what you asked for rather than with what you hope happened, and to write the unmeasured half down beside the measured one.

And prefer reading the definition to running the experiment when the definition is in your node_modules. Two of the four cases here were settled by a source comment and a call site, in less time than a deploy takes, and neither answer could have been reached by watching the tool succeed.

What would change this

A tool that accepts unknown flags silently would break the free half, and the check for that is the bogus-flag control itself: an exit code of 0 on an invented name means every conclusion on this page has to be re-earned with real runs. A hidden flag becoming documented would move its row from this list to an ordinary reference, which is the outcome to hope for. And a measurement showing the capture does honour waitForTimeout would close the one case here that is deliberately still open.

editorial.reader: Someone who has found an undocumented flag or config key and is deciding whether to trust it, having read a description that says what it does and nothing about how it fails.
editorial.problem: An option a tool silently ignores and an option it honours produce the same exit code and the same success. So the ordinary way of checking, which is to send it and see whether the command works, cannot tell those two apart.
editorial.thesis: Acceptance and effect are separate questions, and on a closed schema the first one costs an exit code, so asking it first eliminates the most common way an undocumented option wastes a week.
evidence: The Browser Run payload schema is closed: an unrecognised key comes back as unrecognized_keys, and an invented engine name returns the byte-identical error, so acceptance is answerable with no render performed.

The zstd dictionary option is honoured by node 26, ignored silently by workerd, and was ignored by bun through 1.3.14, with every failure invisible because a frame compressed without a dictionary still decodes with one.
The hidden --max-versions flag defaults to 2 and its own source comment places the limit on the server, which answers a question about the release path by reading rather than by deploying.
The --old-asset-ttl flag reads like a repair for split-deployment asset 404s and is threaded into the legacy Workers Sites sync alone, which this site does not run.
editorial.uncertainty: Whether the Browser Run capture honours waitForTimeout is still open: the key is accepted, and acceptance is the half that was free to measure. A tool that accepted invented flag names would break the cheap control outright, so the bogus-flag probe is the assumption everything here rests on.

understanding.intro: Six questions on the controls, and one on what would break them.

questions.q: Why can sending an option and seeing the command succeed fail to tell you anything?

options.t: A tool that drops an unknown option produces the same success as one that honoured it.
options.why: Right. Success is compatible with both outcomes, so it discriminates between nothing.

options.t: Exit codes report only that the process started, before any option is parsed.
options.why: The exit code is accurate about whether the command worked. The gap is that the command works either way.

options.t: Hidden options apply asynchronously, after the process has already exited 0.
options.why: Nothing here defers option handling past the run. The problem is what a success is evidence for.

questions.q: What makes a closed payload schema useful rather than annoying?

options.t: It refuses an unknown key before any render runs, so probing acceptance is free.
options.why: Right. Validation ahead of execution is what turns the schema into a cheap oracle.

options.t: It guarantees that any key the schema accepts also changes how the render behaves.
options.why: Acceptance and effect stay separate. A closed schema answers the first question only.

options.t: Its error lists every key it accepts, so it doubles as documentation.
options.why: The error names the key it refused and nothing more. It publishes nothing about what it does know.

questions.q: The dictionary control runs three times: no option, the right value, a wrong value. Why run the wrong value at all?

options.t: It ties the smaller output to the value you passed rather than to some other cause.
options.why: Right. Two runs can only show that something differed. The third says the difference tracks the value you supplied.

options.t: It confirms the engine rejects an invalid dictionary instead of ignoring it.
options.why: This control expects the wrong value to be accepted. A rejection would be a different experiment.

options.t: It warms zstd's cache so the other two runs are timed on equal footing.
options.why: The measurement is output size rather than time, so warming buys nothing here.

questions.q: The --max-versions definition sets a default of 2 and carries a comment about a server-side limitation. What follows?

options.t: The server holds the cap, so raising it locally buys an error.
options.why: Right. The flag mirrors a server limit, so the client is the wrong place to argue with it.

options.t: The flag is a leftover, and wrangler ignores whatever number it gets.
options.why: It works as designed. It exposes a client-side knob for a value the server also enforces.

options.t: Passing 3 would let the release script name three versions in one step.
options.why: The comment points at the server refusing, so a higher number surfaces as an error and the split stays at two.

questions.q: --old-asset-ttl is described as keeping old assets alive rather than deleting them. Why did it turn out to be irrelevant here?

options.t: Its one call site is the legacy Workers Sites sync, a layer this site doesn't run.
options.why: Right. The description was accurate about a subsystem that is not running, which a description cannot tell you.

options.t: Wrangler caps the TTL at 60 seconds, too short to cover a gradual rollout.
options.why: No cap was involved. The flag never reaches the code path in question.

options.t: Content-hashed assets are never deleted on a deploy, so a TTL has nothing to delay.
options.why: Content addressing changes the names rather than the deletion behaviour, and it is a separate mechanism from this flag.

questions.q: A 200 comes back from an endpoint you sent an undocumented parameter to. What is the honest label for the result?

options.t: Label it with what was requested, and note the effect as unverified.
options.why: Right. The request is a fact and the effect is a hypothesis, so the label should carry only the first.

options.t: Label it with the engine, since a 200 means it was honoured.
options.why: That is the mislabel this page describes. An endpoint ignoring the parameter returns the same success.

options.t: Discard it, because a 200 from that endpoint carries no information at all.
options.why: It does tell you the request was well formed and that the endpoint served. It just fails to say which engine served it.

questions.q: Which observation would undermine every cheap control on this page?

options.t: A tool exiting 0 on a flag name invented on the spot.
options.why: Right. That would mean acceptance carries no information, and each conclusion would need a real run to re-earn.

options.t: A hidden flag like --max-versions moving into the documented help output.
options.why: That moves a row to an ordinary reference page, which is the good outcome.

options.t: A hidden flag's description contradicting what its code does.
options.why: The page already assumes descriptions are unreliable, which is why the controls read behaviour instead.
